newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian govt battles newly leftist oppn.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian govt battles newly leftist oppn.

text.p: The Australian Labor Party, now in opposition, is reversing its commitment to tough economic reforms, imperilling the new government's capacity to extend the work that Labor pushed through during 13 years in power.

The Liberal-National government has even more zeal for reform than Labor had but analysts say it finds itself without the occasional political support that it gave Labor from the opposition benches in the 1980s and early 1990s.

Labor's reformist prime ministers Bob Hawke and Paul Keating have left the political stage and the party is increasingly hostile to the sort of tough measures it once championed -- tariff cuts, budget cuts, asset sales, a more flexible labour market and painful job losses to improve business efficiency.
"When Labor pursued reforms it generally got the support of the opposition," political analyst Malcolm Mackerras said.
"Now the coalition cannot bring in economic reforms because they don't get the support of Labor," Mackerras, from the Australian Defence Force Academy, told Reuters.
Economists say that faster economic growth will deliver the extra jobs that Australia needs, but sustainable low-inflation growth will come only by boosting efficiency.
So, for example, business leaders are urging Prime Minister John Howard to reform the tax system, particularly by introducing a new value-added tax on consumption.
Labor, sensing a chance to improve its abysmal opinion poll standing, declares implacable opposition to the tax while Howard remains non-committal.
A year after voters crushed Labor in Howard's landslide election win the party is still eight or nine percentage points behind the government in opinion polls.
Since the government does not control the upper house of parliament and almost all non-government senators take leftist positions, many economic reforms cannot survive without opposition support.
Before the election, Opposition Leader Kim Beazley was one of the most reformist of the Labor government's ministers.

He presided over a reshaping of the telecommunications industry -- exposing the government-owned monopoly to private competition -- and immediately before the election he was the minister responsible for selling government assets.
But two forces have pushed Beazley and his party leftwards.
Firstly, the party needs to score political points by deriding the policies of a conservative government. Necessarily, this means taking leftist positions.

Secondly, said Mackerras and fellow analyst Antony Green, politicians since the early 1980s had pushed reform far beyond what the voters wanted -- the centre of political debate had moved far to the right of the average reform-weary voter.
"Political opinion for the past 15 years has been well ahead of where the public is," said Green.

The analysts said this had manifested itself in the crushing defeat of Labor in 1996, which followed Labor unexpectedly hanging onto power in 1993 because of a radically reformist set of Liberal-National policies.

And in late 1996 politicians were surprised by the country being suddenly obsessed with independent member of parliament Pauline Hanson, who carried an anti-reform, anti-immigrant message that they had thought was too simplistic for voters.
Mackerras thought both sides of politics had detected the changed mood and even the conservatives had toned down their ambitions.
"John Howard has obviously made the decision to not be ahead of the voters and Labor has made a similar decision," he said.
